UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                  BEFORE THE
                    FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Southwest Power Pool, Inc.                       )          Docket No. ER26-2249-002
                                                 )

                            PROTEST OF THE
             SOUTHWEST POWER POOL TRANSMISSION OWNER GROUP

         Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s Rules and

Regulations, 1 American Electric Power Service Corporation, as agent for Public Service Company

of Oklahoma and Southwestern Electric Power Company (collectively, AEP), the Evergy

Companies (Evergy), Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (OG&E), 2 and Xcel Energy Services

Inc. on behalf of Southwestern Public Service Company (SPS, together with AEP, Evergy, and

OG&E, the SPP TO Group) submit the following protest against the Response to Request for

Additional Information 3 that Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (SPP) filed on September 18, 2026. 4 The

Response does not adequately address the Commission’s Deficiency Letter and arguments raised

in the SPP TO Group’s pleadings, which highlighted critical deficiencies in SPP’s Peak Demand

Assessment (PDA).

         The Commission gave SPP four topics for which it requested additional information about

SPP’s PDA and Demand Response Resource filing. Despite giving SPP the opportunity to clarify

its proposal, SPP has read the Deficiency Letter as narrowly as possible to sidestep the points the


1

2
  OG&E will be submitting a separate pleading addressing the Demand Response Resource
component of SPP’s proposal.
3
  The SPP TO Group refers to the Request for Additional Information as the “Deficiency Letter”
throughout this Protest. See Deficiency Letter, Docket No. ER26-2249 (Aug. 19, 2026).
4

 SPP TO Group raised in its initial Protest 5 and Limited Answer. 6 Indeed, the central focus of the

SPP TO Group’s arguments—the Demand Adjustment or “error tolerance”—is mentioned only

one time in SPP’s responses despite being the preeminent concern among the “additional

adjustments” addressed in Commission Question 3. SPP’s Response is deficient because it is

incomplete and nonresponsive. SPP has not fixed the clear errors in its proposal, which continues

to be unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory for the same reasons the SPP TO Group

explained in its initial Protest and again in its Limited Answer. 7

          The Commission gave SPP a direct opportunity to justify the Demand Adjustment. SPP

did not do so.       The Commission specifically required SPP to explain why its “additional

adjustments” are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. 8 Yet SPP

referenced the Demand Adjustment only once and offered no substantive justification for assigning

dramatically different tolerances based solely on a Load Responsible Entity’s (LRE) size. SPP

instead devoted its Response to whether the Demand Adjustment may be housed outside the

Tariff. 9 That deliberate narrowing leaves the decisive issue unanswered. The Demand Adjustment

does not impose a uniform standard of forecasting accountability. It creates three different

standards: the smallest LREs receive an error allowance of 50%; midsize LREs receive 2% plus 5

 MW; and LREs at or above 500 MW receive only 3%. 10 The practical consequence is to make the

largest LREs substantially more likely to incur Deficiency Payments while making smaller LREs

substantially less likely to incur those payments and better positioned to receive the resulting

revenues. SPP has not explained why LRE size is a legitimate basis for that disparate treatment.

Because it cannot justify the defining feature of the PDA, its filing remains deficient and the PDA

must be rejected.

I.        PROTEST

          The Commission required SPP to respond to a number of questions addressing four specific

areas of its PDA filing: (1) the effective date of its filing; (2) the contours of the proposal’s weather

normalization methodology; (3) SPP’s proposed “additional adjustments” to the Post-Season Net

Peak Demand; and (4) how Firm Service Level for Demand Response Resources will be

calculated. The Demand Adjustment is one of the “additional adjustments” at issue in Commission

Question 3. As relevant, SPP needed to answer: (a) “why it is just and reasonable and not unduly

discriminatory or preferential for SPP to apply ‘additional adjustments,’ whether upwards

adjustments or downwards adjustments, to the calculation of Post-Season Net Peak Demand;”

(b) “how and when market participants and/or LREs will be informed of any ‘additional

adjustments’ to Post-Season Net Peak Demand;” and (c) “whether, and how, SPP will evaluate

whether ‘additional adjustments’ to Post-Season Net Peak Demand are necessary.” 11

          SPP has failed to answer Commission Question 3 completely. The Commission asked SPP

to justify the substance of its additional adjustments: why they are “just and reasonable and not




10
     See Business Practice 8600 § 2.
11
     Deficiency Letter at 4.


                                                   3
 unduly discriminatory or preferential.” 12 SPP instead answered a different question: whether

details concerning those adjustments may be placed in its Business Practices. 13 That response fails

twice. It does not justify the disparate treatment created by the Demand Adjustment, and it does

not cure the separate rule-of-reason problem created by omitting a determinative component of the

Deficiency Payment framework from the Tariff.

           A.    SPP Failed to Justify the Demand Adjustment’s Facially Discriminatory
                 Treatment

           The Commission required SPP to “explain why it is just and reasonable and not unduly

discriminatory or preferential for SPP to apply ‘additional adjustments,’ whether upwards

adjustments or downwards adjustments, to the calculation of Post-Season Net Peak Demand.” 14

That is a question about the substance of SPP’s proposal. But SPP only responds to a question

that the Commission did not ask: whether its additional adjustments are appropriately placed in

its Business Practices rather than the Tariff. 15 SPP nowhere explains why SPP may impose

materially different forecasting tolerances on LREs performing the same function, or why smaller

LREs receiving the most generous tolerances should remain eligible to receive Deficiency

Payment revenues generated under the stricter standard imposed on larger LREs. SPP’s answer is

therefore not merely incomplete; it is nonresponsive to the substantive inquiry the Commission

posed. SPP cannot satisfy its burden under section 205 by demonstrating that other RTOs place

implementation details in manuals. SPP must demonstrate that this particular rate design is just,

reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory. It has not done so.



12
     Id.
13
     See Response at 25-26.
14
     Deficiency Letter at 4.
15
     See Response at 25-26.


                                                 4
           SPP’s silence on the merits is consequential. It has now had its initial filing, its answer,

and its response to the Commission’s Deficiency Letter to identify a legitimate basis for treating

similarly situated LREs differently according to size. It has identified none. SPP has not shown

that larger LREs forecast less accurately, create greater reliability risks, or are otherwise differently

situated with respect to the objective the PDA purports to advance. Nor has SPP explained why

smaller LREs require allowances that reach 50% when the largest LREs receive only 3%. 16

Without evidence connecting those classifications to a legitimate difference relevant to forecasting

accountability, the classifications are arbitrary and the resulting rate is unduly discriminatory.

          SPP cannot show that its “additional adjustments” are just and reasonable and not unduly

discriminatory until it removes the Demand Adjustment from the PDA. The practical effect of

the Demand Adjustment is that the largest SPP LREs will be materially more likely to incur

Deficiency Payments, while making small and midsize LREs materially more likely to be treated

as having excess capacity eligible for revenue distributions. In short, the smaller LREs will not

only avoid any material risk of paying Deficiency Payments under the PDA, but will also stand to

receive Deficiency Payments from large LREs. That is not forecasting accountability. It is a tiered

system in which accountability decreases as the size of the LRE decreases. 17 SPP has offered no

evidence that forecasting accuracy becomes more difficult as an LRE grows or that a megawatt of

unforecasted load creates less reliability risk when served by a cooperative or municipal utility.



16
     See Business Practice 8600 § 2.
17
  The Clean Energy Organizations (CEOs) and SPP’s Independent Market Monitoring Unit both
correctly observe that the Demand Adjustment “directly reduces an LRE’s post-season obligation
and increases SPP’s exposure to reliability risk without mitigation.” Clean Energy Organization’s
Protest of Southwest Power Pool’s Updated Demand Response and Peak Demand Assessment
Proposal, Docket No. ER26-2249-002 at 4 (Oct. 9, 2026). CEOs also correctly note that the
Demand Adjustment creates an incentive to “overstate weather sensitivity to reduce their potential
exposure to deficiency payments.” Id. at 5.


                                                   5
 The Demand Adjustment distinguishes among LREs based on size, but SPP has not connected that

distinction to the purpose of the PDA.

          The discrimination operates on both sides of the transaction.         The generous error

allowances act as a shield by reducing the likelihood that small and midsize LREs will incur

Deficiency Payments. At the same time, the allowances improve those LREs’ position to hold

excess capacity and share in revenues collected from deficient LREs. The same classification that

protects smaller LREs from paying thus enhances their opportunity to receive payments generated

by the stricter standard imposed on larger LREs. SPP has not justified either side of that

arrangement, much less their combined effect. A rate design that assigns one class the narrowest

margin for error and another class both a de facto exemption and a potential financial benefit is

not rendered just and reasonable by labeling the classifications an “error tolerance.”

         B.      The Votes of the PDA’s Intended Beneficiaries Cannot Justify the
                 Discriminatory Treatment

          The stakeholder history confirms that the discriminatory treatment is not incidental to the

proposal. The proposal obtained the stakeholder support necessary to advance because the

cooperative and municipal entities receiving its most favorable treatment overwhelmingly

supported it, while the investor-owned utilities exposed to its most meaningful financial risk

overwhelmingly opposed it.         As the SPP TO Group previously explained, smaller LREs

responsible for serving only 8% of total SPP load secured for themselves a de facto Deficiency

Payment exemption and potential award while shifting forecasting responsibility and Deficiency

Payment exposure to the larger LREs. 18 SPP therefore cannot invoke stakeholder approval as

evidence that the PDA is just and reasonable. The votes of the proposal’s intended beneficiaries



18
     Protest at 30.


                                                   6
 confirm the advantage the mechanism confers, but they do not supply a lawful justification for that

advantage.

          At MOPC, 85% of cooperatives and 83% of municipal utilities supported RR703,

compared with only 7% of investor-owned utilities. A proposal to remove the PDA’s Deficiency

Payment provisions received 64% support representing at least 80% of SPP load but nevertheless

failed under the stakeholder voting structure. The Members Committee then rejected RR703 by a

vote of 12 to 4. SPP’s generalized reference to stakeholder approval therefore conceals the more

relevant fact—the proposal advanced through the stakeholder process on the votes of the entities

it favored, over the opposition of entities serving most of the affected load.

          That voting outcome cannot make the Demand Adjustment lawful. The Commission’s

independent review exists to prevent a stakeholder majority from using an RTO process to assign

itself preferential treatment at the expense of an outnumbered minority. The cooperative and

municipal votes may explain how the Demand Adjustment survived the stakeholder process. They

do not explain why its disparate treatment is just and reasonable. 19 The resulting transfer is also

squarely inconsistent with El Paso Electric Co. v. FERC, 20 where the Fifth Circuit rejected an

allocation framework that specifically and intentionally designated non-jurisdictional utilities as


19
   The Federal Power Act does not permit FERC to substitute stakeholder preferences for the
Commission's own statutory judgment. The D.C. Circuit has long held that FERC must
independently determine whether a filed rate is just and reasonable, regardless of the degree of
industry support. See, e.g., Laclede Gas Co. v. FERC, 873 F.2d 1494, 1498 (D.C. Cir. 1989). The
Commission itself has repeatedly held that stakeholder support, even broad stakeholder consensus,
cannot ultimately prove that a rate design is just and reasonable,” Am. Elec. Power Serv. Corp. v.
Midwest Indep. Transmission Sys. Operator, Inc., 122 FERC ¶ 61,083, at P 172 (2008), that the
Commission does not consider stakeholder support “dispositive as to whether a proposal is just
and reasonable,” N.Y. Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 158 FERC ¶ 61,064, at P 58 (2017), and that
while the Commission “accord[s] an appropriate degree of deference to RTO stakeholder
processes, [the Commission’s] decisions are based on [its] review of the record,” Sw. Power Pool,
Inc., 152 FERC ¶ 61,226, at P 116 (2015).
20
     76 F.4th 352 (5th Cir. 2023).


                                                  7
 beneficiaries while imposing costs on jurisdictional utilities. 21 The PDA presents the same

fundamental defect: it uses size-based allowances to make smaller, frequently non-jurisdictional

LREs the intended beneficiaries of payments funded disproportionately by larger, Commission-

jurisdictional LREs.

      C.      Even Apart from Its Substantive Discrimination, the Demand Adjustment
              Violates the Rule of Reason

       The Demand Adjustment must be rejected because it is substantively discriminatory.

Independently, SPP also cannot enforce that mechanism without placing its material terms in the

Tariff. Throughout its Response, SPP says that it proposes to incorporate its Business Practices

into the Tariff via compliance filing “to the extent the Commission is concerned” that its

requirements do not satisfy the rule of reason. 22 The Commission should require that for two

reasons: first, because the Demand Adjustment is clearly the sort of material money-shifting

provision that belongs in the Tariff, not the Business Practices and, second, because stakeholders

must be able to read the language that SPP actually proposes to incorporate into the Tariff.

Currently, there is insufficient detail in the Tariff or SPP’s proposed Tariff language to satisfy the

rule of reason.




21
   As the Fifth Circuit explained, see id. at 362, the Commission “may never approve unjust and
unreasonable rates by allocating costs to those who reap little to no benefit, see Ill. Com. Comm'n
[v. FERC], 576 F.3d [470] at 476 [(7th Cir. 2009)], nor may it choose not to allocate costs to ‘those
who cause the costs to be incurred and reap the resulting benefits.’ Nat'l Ass'n of Reg. Util.
Comm'rs [v. FERC], 475 F.3d at 1285 [(D.C. Cir. 2003)] (emphasis added); see also Consol.
Edison Co. of NY v. FERC, 45 F.4th 265, 282 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (per curiam) (vacating portion of
FERC order that exempted “de minimis” beneficiaries from cost allocation).”
22
  See Response at 25-27 (quoting 76 F.4th 352, 361 (5th Cir. 2023)); id. at 27-29 (citing, e.g.,
Consol. Edison Co. of N.Y., Inc. v. FERC, 45 F.4th 265 (D.C. Cir. 2022)).


                                                  8
          The Demand Adjustment is itself a rate, not a “mere implementation detail,” 23 because it

acts as a trigger for money to change hands between LREs who pay Deficiency Payments and

those who receive them. As such, it must be included in the Tariff, but it has not been. As the

SPP TO Group has explained, the PDA does not “‘broadly describe the process and procedures to

be used’ in such a way as to comply with the Commission’s rules for incorporating a manual by

reference because it fails to outline a mechanism that will prove determinative of whether an LRE

will be subject to Deficiency Payments.” 24 The Tariff, as it currently stands, does not incorporate

the relevant Business Practices governing the Demand Adjustment nor does it provide notice that

the Demand Adjustment even exists. SPP is certainly aware of its obligations to provide adequate

notice under the Tariff because the Commission previously rejected SPP’s 2022 ELCC revisions

on the basis that SPP failed to “set forth the process to be used and outline[] parameters for

calculations” in the Tariff. 25

         While it is helpful that SPP has attached the Business Practices to this filing, that is not

sufficient to satisfy the rule of reason, as SPP recognizes by its proposal to submit a compliance

filing if requested. In any compliance filing, SPP must identify in the Tariff the relevant manual

being incorporated, state clearly that it is incorporating those Business Practices into the Tariff,

and provide sufficient detail and clarity in its explanation of the Demand Adjustment so that SPP’s

stakeholders can evaluate their rights and obligations.

         But even full disclosure would only reveal the discrimination more clearly. It would not

make the discrimination lawful. SPP’s proposed compliance filing is therefore not a remedy to


23
     Hecate Energy Greene Cty. 3 LLC v. FERC, 72 F.4th 1307, 1312 (D.C. Cir. 2023).
24
  Protest at 35 (quoting Sw. Power Pool, Inc., 180 FERC ¶ 61,074, at P 26 (2022), reh’g granted,
182 FERC ¶ 61,100 (2023)).
25
     Sw. Power Pool, 180 FERC ¶ 61,074 at P 26.


                                                  9
 SPP’s facially discriminatory Demand Adjustment. The Commission cannot accept an unjust and

unreasonable rate subject to SPP later writing that same rate more clearly. The rule-of-reason

defect requires rejection of the incomplete Tariff provisions; the independent discrimination defect

requires rejection of the PDA and Demand Adjustment in total.

       Ultimately, SPP’s Response confirms that the Commission cannot resolve this proceeding

through a compliance filing. SPP did not justify the Demand Adjustment’s disparate treatment,

did not identify a legitimate forecasting or reliability distinction corresponding to its size-based

classifications, and did not explain why entities receiving de facto protection from Deficiency

Payments should remain eligible to receive revenues collected under the stricter standard imposed

on larger LREs. SPP instead proposes to preserve the same functional design and place more of

its terms in the Tariff. That would cure neither the discrimination nor SPP’s failure to carry its

burden under section 205. The Commission should reject the PDA outright and direct SPP to

develop a framework that imposes forecasting accountability on a reasonable and

nondiscriminatory basis.

                                          CONCLUSION

       For these reasons, the Commission should reject SPP’s attempt to file an unduly

discriminatory rate and reject SPP’s offer to cure its failure to observe the rule of reason through

a compliance filing. SPP has not answered the Deficiency Letter’s central inquiry, has not justified

the Demand Adjustment’s preferential treatment of smaller LREs, and has not filed the material

terms of the mechanism in its Tariff. The PDA is unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory

and should be rejected in its entirety.

         Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s Rules and

Regulations, 1 American Electric Power Service Corporation, as agent for Public Service Company

of Oklahoma and Southwestern Electric Power Company (collectively, AEP), the Evergy

Companies (Evergy), Oklahoma Gas and Electric Company (OG&E), and Xcel Energy Services

Inc. on behalf of Southwestern Public Service Company (SPS, together with AEP, Evergy, and

OG&E, the SPP TO Group) submit the following protest against the Peak Demand Assessment

(PDA) framework that Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (SPP) proposed to implement in the SPP East

Balancing Authority Area (BAA) on April 17, 2026, 2 as amended to include the SPP West BAA

on May 6, 2026. 3 The SPP TO Group supports improvements to load forecasting, but opposes the

PDA because it creates a new and counterproductive load forecasting penalty system that unduly

discriminates against Load Responsible Entities (LREs) 4 with larger loads while effectively

excusing small LREs from accurate load forecasting through a complex web of exemptions.

        The PDA is a shell game designed to give the false impression of improving load

forecasting, but it is a complex mechanism to excuse small LREs from load forecasting penalties

that they face under SPP’s current resource adequacy construct. The new PDA shifts the entire

burden of load-forecasting accuracy to large LREs. SPP’s PDA is both facially discriminatory and

ineffective for its stated objective. SPP bases its PDA on the false assumption that LREs are not

currently incentivized to forecast load accurately. But, imposing Deficiency Payments on a post-

season basis will not improve load forecasts. In reality, LREs have countless reasons to get their

load forecasts right.   Moreover, SPP is overwhelmingly composed of vertically-integrated

utilities—including the SPP TO Group—who work hand in hand with their state regulators to

develop integrated resource plans (IRPs) to address resource adequacy needs for the retail

customers in their respective jurisdictions. And it is state regulators, not the LREs, that approve

the quantity and types of generation that LREs ultimately acquire to serve load. It makes no sense

to punish LREs for employing load forecasts reviewed by state regulators that also exercise control

through retail load management oversight.

       The SPP TO Group further opposes the PDA because the mechanism by which SPP adjusts

Post-Season Net Peak Demand, i.e., the Demand Adjustment, is a wealth transfer tool designed to

provide the illusion of more effective load forecasting. The Demand Adjustment excuses the

overwhelming majority of SPP LREs from having to pay Deficiency Payments by creating a

complex web of de facto exemptions based on a utility’s size, thus leaving the SPP TO Group to

carry Deficiency Payments on behalf of the region merely because they serve larger loads than

other LREs. The SPP TO Group is not alone in recognizing this, as SPP’s Market Monitoring Unit

similarly emphasizes that the Demand Adjustment will “allow LREs to consistently fall short of

their calculated contribution to maintain regional reliability RARs without financial




                                                2
 consequence.” 5 It is no surprise that the smaller, non-Commission jurisdictional LREs with the

most to gain from the Demand Adjustment voted to impose it on less numerous large utilities

during the stakeholder process. In addition, the PDA violates the Commission’s “rule of reason”

by placing the Demand Adjustment mechanism entirely within SPP’s Business Practice Manual

8600.

          The PDA proposal is deeply flawed. SPP requested an effective date of January 1, 2027

to delay implementation of the PDA until the 2028 Summer Reliability Assessment Plan. Given

the lack of urgency, the Commission should deny SPP’s proposal and let stakeholders develop a

solution to under-forecasting load that actually addresses the perceived problem and refrains from

grossly discriminatory and unlawful exemptions.

I.        BACKGROUND

         A.         SPP Load Forecasting

          SPP’s Resource Adequacy framework is set out in Attachment AA of SPP’s Open Access

Transmission Tariff (Tariff). Under that framework, LREs must procure enough capacity to meet

their Resource Adequacy Requirement (RAR) for both the Winter and Summer Seasons or face

Deficiency Payments. 6 Under SPP’s existing structure, LREs submit workbooks reflecting their

available capacity before the start of the applicable season that SPP then uses to verify compliance

with the RAR for the upcoming season. 7 This pre-season requirement is financially binding in

that LREs that fail to satisfy their RARs are assessed Deficiency Payments based on forecasted




5
 Protest of the Southwest Power Pool Market Monitoring Unit, Docket No. ER26-2249 at 21 (May
11, 2026) (MMU Protest).
6
